utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [French on English channel]

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: French came over the English channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now it should be okay. Yes, Ms. West, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Guzina.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: When we finished last Thursday, you had just testified that there were no sniper rifles in your battalion. You said that you had no need for it because the confrontation -- can you hear me in a language --

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you speak up a bit, just a bit louder, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Our usher will assist you in turning up the volume for your headphone. Mr. Guzina --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- do you hear me well now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So when we spoke last on Thursday you had just finished telling us that there were no sniper rifles in your battalion and you had no need for sniper rifles because the confrontation line was so close. And you also said that when you were confronted about snipers by UNPROFOR, you of course denied that you had snipers. Do you remember testifying about this?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that in that part of Nedzarici I did not have any snipers, but it is a fact that I had M48 rifles with optic sights, and I think that in the 4th Company of my battalion there were three snipers that were pointed in the completely opposite direction, Butmir, the airport, not the locations that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have P01739.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So now I see that you say you had M48 rifles with optic sights, and so were those rifles used for sniping?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You also say that you had -- in the 4th Company of your battalion there were three snipers that were pointed in the completely opposite direction, at the airport, not the locations that you mentioned. I didn't mention any locations. I was talking about snipers generally. So when I asked you last week whether you had snipers, you didn't tell us about these particular snipers, did you?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously we did not understand each other then. The fact is that in terms of these examples of incidents that had occurred, it all has to do with Nedzarici, so I was thinking along those lines, namely, that in Nedzarici there weren't any snipers and there was no mention of targets in Butmir, I mean that is where the snipers were turned and that is why we were thinking at cross-purposes, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Since you and I spoke on Thursday, have you discussed your testimony with anyone?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So may we have P01739.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is the map that we looked at last week and you had identified for me that number 7, the red dot number 7, you recognised to be what you understood to be the location of the sniping incident described as F7. And you also said for us last week that number 75 on the left-hand side of the screen you recognised to be the theological institute. Now, in your statement in regard to this scheduled incident, you indicated that the theological institute was about 1.500 metres from F7; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But the confrontation line between the area of Dobrinja and the area of your responsibility was much closer, wasn't it, it was about 550 metres to F7; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you say it's that way, then it's probably that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have P1621, please, e-court page 54. P1621. For the record, this is the Prosecution expert sniping report.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, I know you - e-court page 54, please - grew up in this area and obviously spent a lot of time in this area. This is a satellite image of the area we just spoke about. To the extreme right where the little blue dot is, that's F7, that's the same -- that's the red dot you just looked at. And as we go to the left you see 550 metres, that would be the confrontation line, and the green area is where the screen is set up. Does this satellite imagery at least look familiar to you? Does this look like the area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we zoom on the upper page only so that we can see a bit better?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can go to e-court page 53, the page right before it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I want to share with you some of the information the Trial Chamber has received and this regards that particular incident and the opinion of this person. He said the range -- towards the bottom of the page in the English. He said the range of this sniping fire was more than 550 metres, more likely to be more than 700 metres, and a scope will probably have been used --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, I take it we have a translation --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Indeed, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So this -- so we have both the English right now. There we go. So on the left-hand side you will see the B/C/S version and towards the bottom it talks about the range. It's the third complete paragraph from the bottom, indicating that it was more than 550 metres, more likely more than 700 metres, and a scope was probably used. And then the next paragraph says: "The round will probably have been a 7.62-millimetre or 7.92-millimetre calibre and have been fired from an M76 or M91 sniper rifle." Now, I know you just mentioned that you did have -- I think you said it was an M48. Did you have any M76 rifles in your battalion?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember what type of rifle that is. Could you tell me a bit more about that? I'm not a military expert. I'm simply one of the ordinary people who became a commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And we can talk about that a little bit more. But in the meanwhile putting aside the suggestion that the round for F7 that this incident came from the theological institute, if I told you the source of fire was more likely to be more than 550 metres beyond the confrontation line, would you then agree with me that more than 550 metres means the source of the round was from SRK territory?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, possibly the source of fire was from the area of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, but I claim with full responsibility that there was no sniper activity from the theological faculty, because we had heavy machine-guns there, PAT Brownings. We didn't have snipers up there. And I claim with full responsibility that no one could have fired a sniper bullet within the zone of the 1st Battalion from the faculty of theology. Those are facts. All the rest is false. I could understand if you were speaking about other positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 23830, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So this is a document of the Ilidza Brigade and it's dated October 1993. And you see the B/C/S already on the left and we'll see the English shortly. This is a document to the corps command in which -- from the Ilidza Brigade. It says that: "This unit has 30 sniper rifles in total (of which, 15," and I believe it's M "76 and 15 are M48). "We also have one silencer and one passive infrared device. "So far we have deployed 16 soldiers in combat. "We ask you to send us the silencers for all the sniper rifles in our possession." Now you've already said that your battalion had the M48 rifles. What about M76? Does this help you remember a little bit more?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a moment ago that I had M48 and three M76 rifles but pointed at Butmir. That is the area across the airport runway.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: My apologies. I didn't realise that you said there were M76. So you concede that you had both M48 and M76 sniper rifles?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said a moment ago, that we had M48 and M76, but these M76 rifles were in the 4th Company and were pointed at Butmir, opposite the airport, because we had constant sniper activity along Kasindolska Street from the area of Butmir and we exclusively pointed our sniper rifles in that direction and the people who were operating them, but the fact remains that we did not have any trained people.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. And you then, I'm sure, will agree with the proposition that this Trial Chamber heard at transcript 6940 from the expert Prosecution sniping witness that an M76 was a standard sniper rifle; that's true, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that's true. If you say that it's that name, then it's probably that name. I'm no expert as far as weapons are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document has already been admitted as P6014. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I now want to move to F9 and this is your paragraph 45 of your statement in which you discuss F9. And this was the incident that took place on Djure Jaksica Street. May we have P01803, please. This is the Sarajevo map book and I just want you to take a look at the area. We're looking for map 9, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Perhaps that is another document. This document has only one map and this is the one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Maybe it'll be even better to go to your exhibit, which is 1D10070, please, and this is your own map and so you'll be familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: 1D10070, that's the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And this is the map in which you showed the confrontation line around your area so you'll recognise it. Very good.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now if we could -- Mr. Usher, can you change over the witness's screen so that he can mark on it, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, looking at this map can you identify where the school for the blind is? And you can circle that.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you also understand from your statement that the event -- the incident of F9 took place on Djure Jaksica Street, but that street's name has now changed, has it not, to Adija Mulabegovica Street; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. I don't go to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And we see that street where you just drew the circle, it's very close to the right side of the circle, right? You see Adilja Mulabegovica Street, right? Look up at the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And the allegation of this sniping incident is that it happened almost at the end so that the distance between the school of the blind and the alleged incident was about 200 metres, was it not?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So in your statement at paragraph 5 -- excuse me, 45, where you spoke about this, you said that: "I can say with regard to this that the place of the alleged incident was behind the first line and that it was not logical to assume the presence of civilians in this location." Tell us why it was not logical to assume that civilians would be located there?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the date itself, the 26th of June, 1994, is very telling; that is to say, all people who lived in Alipasino Polje knew where the separation lines were and it is a fact that they knew that this is the worst line during the conflict between the Serbs and Muslims. That is to say, even the sparrows that were flying in that area knew that that was the worst area. So I don't understand, therefore, why civilians would go out risking their lives.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could other microphones please be switched off when the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So those are the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: In paragraph 39 of your statement you spoke about civilians being on the separation lines as well, and you said in paragraph 39: "There were no civilians on the lines of disengagement or, at least, there should not have been any. Each komandir or komandant was supposed to evacuate the civilians from the zones of combat operations," or limit their presence in the zones. "It sometimes happened in my zone that civilians" - and here you speak about Serbs - "constantly turned up near the first lines, despite all warnings and prohibitions. The reason for such behaviour was a wish to be in their homes and to take care of their property. This could well have been the case on the other side of the conflict line, and this is why a large number of civilians became casualties." So, sir, in paragraph 45 you said it wasn't logical for them to be there, yet in paragraph 39 you give a good reason why they would be here. But my question is this: Isn't it true that the reason civilians were on the confrontation lines was because front line or not, civilians lived in that area; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that civilians lived in that area, or rather, came to that area, if say they had an apartment in that area and if they had lived there before the conflict broke out. But the fact remains, especially with regard to incident F9, the fact remains that in the corps documents it says that on the 25th and the 26th there was fierce fighting in the area. That is to say that there was strong gun-fire there too. And the fact remains when there is gun-fire or shooting going on, everybody is fleeing, trying to stay alive. And if they're in a shelter then they don't go out. So that's it as far as this incident is concerned. Between the 25th and the 26th, there was -- there was shooting.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What did you say between the 25th and the 26th there was what? Interpreters didn't hear you well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the night between the 25th and the 26th, in the corps documents, 1D6807, regular combat report of the command, it says that there was constant gun-fire from both sides, that there was a fierce attack of the Muslims, and we were fiercely defending ourselves too, and this continued on the 26th of June, that is to say the fighting that continued in that area, and what happened happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. And we're going to come to that document and we'll go through it in detail, but before we get there I want to discuss with you a little bit more about the subject matter of civilians on the front lines. And on Thursday you had mentioned to the Trial Chamber that you had been interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor in 2003. And when you were interviewed you spoke about this very issue. Do you remember what you said?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a long time ago, 2003. Remind me, please, and then ...

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 24281. 65 ter 24281 for the English and the B/C/S has a separate number, Your Honour, and that number for the B/C/S is 24266A, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So what we see on the English page 6, please, and we'll shortly see the B/C/S translation, and that's 24266A, and it's page 3 of the B/C/S. Thank you. It's the middle paragraph in the B/C/S, and I'm going to read out what you said about this particular subject matter and then I'll ask you a question. As regards to civilians on the front line. It's the paragraph beginning: "We also considered that civilian clothing did not render them unsuitable as a target (the men that is) because we knew from intelligence that only about 30 per cent of Bosnian male forces actually possessed a uniform. I also considered that any man or woman that close to the front line (within range of infantry weapons) was a potential target: After all, what were they doing there if they were not a threat? The Muslims, as I have written, were able to go about their business without venturing near the front lines and within range. They could move freely if they had just used their buildings for cover. We had to assume that they constituted a threat." Was this the only assessment you used in determining whether you could legitimately fire at people on the front line?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know yourself, and I've already said that, that a soldier who was at a position was the only person who had the right to decide whether he is under threat or not and whether he is going to fire or not. We told our soldiers that Muslim propaganda was working in all sorts of ways, that they will try to manipulate in different ways, that they will resort to provocations, that they are going to pretend that we are sniping all the time and killing innocent civilians, but I don't think that is true. We did whatever was within our powers.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So let's back up for a moment. You don't deny you said this; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably if it's written here, but whether it's all been translated correctly I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. And --

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that I said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you didn't presume that those people on the front line were civilians in the absence of some specific reason showing they were a threat; right? You didn't make that presumption that people could be civilians?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The soldier in his position first has to make an assumption of whether his position is under threat or not. The point F9 that you are referring to is a place where a civilian has nothing to do. If you look at the students' hall, it's isolated, there are no houses, there are no shops, no market-place. So why would anybody walk across a military field --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- towards the students' hall where a person would be visible from the home for the blind?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So then should we understand that it's your position that any person who walks near the front line is a legitimate target because they have no better reason to be there but be a threat to the SRK?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we have noted that from the Muslim side and the Serbian side we both had the obligation to remove civilians from those lines, and whether at a particular moment, whether it was foggy or raining, a soldier would see a target and make his own decision and would do what he did. You have never been in a war and you can't understand that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's look at an example of civilians on the front lines. We're going to look at F7 which is what you spoke about in your statement, and this is at paragraph 44. But just to understand the background, you grew up in this area; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Ilidza municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You owned a restaurant in this area and you were well familiar with everything in the area; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Sokolovic colony and Ilidzajno [phoen]. However, Alipasino Polje and the area of the 1st Battalion, I came there only when I was appointed and when the war broke out because I had lived before in a completely different area.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, notwithstanding, you were the commander in this particular area so there is no doubt you knew it well. And I'll direct your attention to paragraph 36 where you say the school for the blind and the theology institute were very important facilities in the battalion zone. My predecessor positioned an observation post there and I carried out engineering work to reinforce them. You yourself have been to the school for the blind, have you not?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, many times, and I said that because we had no better positions because the theology institute and the school for the blind were three-storey buildings. If there had been any taller buildings, we would have probably occupied them.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 23970, please. 23970, this is going to be a photo and this photo was taken in 2000. And it's taken from the school of the blind. Mr. President, may I have a moment, please. Mr. Registrar, may we have 24267, please. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is a photo that was taken in 2000 and this is one close-up, but we'll go back in a moment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder whether you are being heard by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We'll back up and I'll show you what the view is with the naked eye, but we are looking at the location of this incident and can you confirm for me that in 1994 this little short building we see in the middle of the photo was not there; that was added after the fact. Correct? That little, I think, restaurant or something.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact is from this viewpoint it looks real to me that there are curtains there and windows. Everything was bullet-ridden at that time. It's a nice picture, but I can't believe that that was the school for the blind.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No, no, no, and what we'll do in a moment is we will back up and I'll show you a larger view which I think will be more helpful and which you can look from the school of the blind to the location at F9.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the war I have never once been in that area so I don't know what it looks like.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: That's fine, sir. Nonetheless we can still look at the photo. But before we do, you earlier -- you mentioned a document and you said during this period of time there had been ongoing fighting.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May I have 1D01762, please. 1D01762.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And this is the document that you mentioned to us earlier in paragraph 45.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1D6807. That's what I see in my copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And this -- the photo -- excuse me, the document you see on the screen -- look at the document you see on the screen, is that the one you recognise, right? This is the report of June 26th, 1994.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's the document I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So let's go through this document to see what it says and how it regards the situation at the time. The report was written at 1700 hours on June 26. And when we start to read it, it says: In the area of responsibility of the Ilidza brigade on June 25th, so the day before, at 2020, so in the evening, the enemy fired one 82-millimetre shell on our positions from the directions of Kopici [phoen]. So we're going to stop right there. Sir, are you aware that the incident of which we speak happened on June 26th at about 7.00 or 7.30 in the evening, almost 24 hours later. Are you aware of that information?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Assuming that that information is true, you would agree with me that the first part of this document, then, does not bear on the firing status almost a day later and is not relevant to what was happening in that particular location almost a day later?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let me read the rest of the sentence and this will help you. It then says at -- and at 2215, so this is still June 25th, they fired two grenades from the direction of Glavogodina on our positions. So this entire sentence regards the events of the previous evening, does it not?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what it relates to, but I stand behind what I said, that on the night between the 25th and the 26th and on the day of the 26th, fighting was going on in the area of the 1st Battalion. I stand by that statement of mine. I found in my notes and my diaries that I kept about day-by-day events in my battalion. This information I did not base myself on the reports of the corps --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- we often did not even send details to the command of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The incident of which we speak happens on the evening of the 26th, not the day of the 26th. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hear that from you now.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And assuming that that information is true, then would you agree with me that this document does not support your suggestion that these incident -- this incident can be attributed to what was going on during the normal course of the war events?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The facts are what I explained to you a moment ago. Whether this document corroborates what I said or not, it does give some details. But the fact is I found in my diaries that on that night and on that day there was combat going on in that area along the whole line and that justifies me saying what I'm saying. I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And when you say "that night," you mean the night of the 25th; and when you say "that day," you mean the day of the 26th. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The night of the 25th, between the 25th and the 26th, and the day of the 26th.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has heard evidence that according to one of the girls in this incident, they had not -- she said that they had not heard any firing that day nor seen troops in the nearby trench. She also said that she walked that route three to four times a week and had not seen soldiers in that portion of the route. This is adjudicated fact 229 and it's from her Galic testimony. Were you aware of that information that I just said before you attested to paragraph 45?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know about that, but the fact is you believe Muslim reports, not Serb ones. That's up to you. I don't believe this happened that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We can move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender that document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it not admitted?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, it's an associated exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, D2554.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's move on from June and work into July -- but first, on Thursday when we spoke about sniping incidents, on Thursday as regards to whether when UNPROFOR approached you and made accusations against your battalion for sniping, what you said in response. And this is at 31157. And I said: Did you deny that you were doing that to UNPROFOR? And you said: "Of course I denied it because I know we did not have any sniper rifles in the area of the 1st Battalion." Now, let's -- putting aside your concessions today about sniper rifles in the area of the 1st Battalion, I'd like to talk about some events in July.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And may I have P1600, please. P1600, page 5 of the English; page 6 of the B/C/S. And we're looking at number 2, please. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And this is warring party activity. This is dated July 11th, and it's an UNMO daily sitrep. And under "warring party activity," number 2 (b), it says: "UNMOs confirm from the spot as well as hospital visit 1 X Bosnian civilian male (age 17) injured by sniping at BP863578 near the house for blind people at Alipasino Polje area at" and it says July 11th. "It is suspected that the sniping came from," and it gives the same B number -- BP number, "the BSA side. It may be highlighted that this is the third casualty (all civilians) in the same spot in last few days." So this is several days after the incident with the girls and this reports at least one sniping being the third casualty in the same spot in the last few days. Mr. Guzina, how do you account for this? You say that your sniping rifles were pointed at Butmir, but at this point we've now seen at least two sniping incidents from the school of the blind not pointed at Butmir?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are trying to say that a military sniper hit that young man, that it was established that the bullet that hit him came from a military sniper. Is that what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No, I want to go back to the document. What the document says is the sniping bullet is coming from the school of the blind and it hit a 17-year-old man. This happened on July 11th. Were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I'm asking you, has it been established that the bullet that hit that 17-year-old boy came from a military sniper? That's what I want to know because I maintain that professional military snipers were not at that position. There were rifles with optic sights, M48, used by soldiers who happened to be in that position at the time. Has it been established that the round was a real sniper round of the appropriate calibre to the sniper rifle?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, sir, we're going to look at another document and then I'm going to ask you whether it's been established or not. But let's focus on the fact -- on not so much sniper rifle but actually on individual shooting at particular people, P1601. This is a document from the very next day. P1601.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'd like to have page 4 in the English, please. And for the B/C/S it's going to be under number 24, paragraph 24 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And this -- from the very next day, other important incidents. Number (b): "Commander of the 1st Battalion of the BSA Ilidza Brigade admitted the sniping by BSA from BP 859578 (house for the blind people). He promised that there would be no more sniping from that place." Mr. Guzina, you were the commander of the 1st Battalion of the BSA Ilidza Brigade, were you not?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to locate that on the screen. I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: 24(b), at the very bottom, and it probably bleeds over into the next page. But do you see that now?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, now I see it. Do you mean that the military observer asked me about this?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly what it says. It says they asked you about it and you did not of course deny it as you told us on Thursday you had done. Instead, you admitted the sniping by BSA positions at the house for the blind, did you not?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this is a report by the military observers?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: My question for you, sir, is: Did you admit that there was sniping from the house for the blind? You can answer that with a yes or no. Please do not answer it with a question.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't see anywhere that I admitted sniping.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I think that's fine we can leave it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, if you are going to put the document, we need to inform the foundation of the document properly. Yes, why don't we show the first page of this document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So this is the UNMO headquarters daily sitrep. And if you go to paragraph 24 and UNMO Sector Sarajevo reports, inter alia, other important incidents. And in subparagraph (b) it says like this, if you take time to read it. And if you are ready, let us know so that we can go to the next page. So do you agree that commander of the 1st Battalion of the Ilidza Brigade was you at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was commander of the 1st Battalion, but I don't see on what basis you claim that I said that. UNPROFOR was able to write whatever they pleased, and in our talks with UNPROFOR we had a liaison officer from UNPROFOR, liaison officers from the UNPROFOR who understood our position - us on the Serb side - but there were other kinds of liaison officer too and it all depends on who wrote this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is not an UNPROFOR report, it's an UNMO report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, to me it's all the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, at paragraph 39 of your report you said you never issued an order to fire at civilians, nor am I aware that any of my subordinates or superiors issued such orders. Did you ever issue an order not to fire at civilians?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did you ever see an order not to fire at civilians issued by your superiors?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in the early days of the war there was a decree from Mr. Karadzic, the president, to take care about civilians and such things.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have 24281, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is your interview in 2003. 24281 is the English, page 4. And then the B/C/S is 24266A, and it's page 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have page 4 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And when asked about this particular subject matter in 2003 -- thank you. It's the paragraph third from the bottom beginning with "when the UNMOs." This is what you said. And right in the middle of that paragraph, and the paragraph in B/C/S is at the top, on left side of the screen, you said: "I can't not remember if they (the Corps) sent me a response to the issue of shooting civilians," and you had just said that you told your superiors, "but certainly we did not receive instructions not to do it or amend the terms by which we engaged targets." And then you say: "I will explain this in detail later." So you just told us that you remembered that there was some sort of decree from Mr. Karadzic to take care about civilians, and you just told us this now, but when asked about this in 2003, you said, "Certainly we did not receive instructions not to do it." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall saying this, but I can say that they also used word games like you are using here. I don't know what I said at that time, whether the interpreter interpreted it correctly. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, what about the rules of engagement, was that something that you discussed with your subordinates and your superiors?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I did not graduate from any military academies, I was not trained to be an officer, I was not trained to be a commander. I learned things as I went during the war from the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So then I should understand then that you never gave any order explaining the rules of engagement to your subordinates, did you?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did issue orders which were carried out. I issued orders with regard to the defence lines of the 1st Battalion. I told them that at no cost those should be threatened and that we had to do everything to preserve the territory and to preserve the municipality of Ilidza. If the lines of the 1st Battalion fell, all of Ilidza would have been threatened, including our families and children. That's why we were engaged in decisive struggle in that area. I can tell you that two brigades and one battalion were in my zone of responsibility, the 102nd and the 155th Brigades and one part of the 104 Brigade. We were a very important area, therefore, and we were engaged in decisive battle in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And when you said I told them at no cost those should be threatened and that we had to do everything to preserve the territory and preserve the municipality of Ilidza, this included shooting at any individual who was on the front line on the Bosnian Muslim side, did it not?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All this time you are trying to make me say that we opened fire on civilians. We did not, never with an intention to kill civilians. However, I'm not saying that there were no mistakes; however, there was never an intention to kill civilians. We never did that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So on Thursday when we were speaking about the bus incident, I asked you whether -- I asked you about targeting and how -- whether it would be easy to hit a stationary bus. And you said at the time, this is 31158: "Well, if this is not a trained sniper shooter, if he were to fire ten bullets at the bus, maybe one or two would hit the target but certainly not all ten." Now, in this particular issue of targeting, you spoke about this as well in your 2003 interview. Do you remember what you said back then?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please jog my memory and then I'll try and remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We are on 24281, the same document we have now. And if we can go to page 5 of the English on the top and for the B/C/S it's page 1 and it's the bottom big paragraph.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not been receiving any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you hear me speak?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. So now looking at this paragraph - and we can scroll down in English so I can see the top, please. "After a few weeks of the war," this is what you said in 2003, "we had all the likely targets registered with a huge degree of accuracy and it was just a case of naming the location and the rounds fell. In the early days until the gunners had their target recorded perfectly, there were instances of rounds landing a small distance off target, but once we had adjusted fire and effectively locked on to target, the gunners were totally accurate. We achieved this accuracy within a few weeks of the start of the war and kept it until the very end. If we wanted a target hitting, we hit it." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about that. I don't know whether everything was interpreted accurately. I don't know that. I can see now that even today there have been some mistakes in the interpretation, let alone here, such a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So could we assume that if you intended to hit a certain location you had the capacity to hit that particular location; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended on the period of the war and on the incident. Can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, you say it depended on the period of war. Here in this statement you indicated that early on in the war you were targeting quite well, so why would it depend on the period of the war. Would you agree with me that later on in the war your targeting would be even better?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly move away from the microphones. He's too close.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right. As the war went on, our targeting got better and better.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: There you go. It was just too loud. Sir, can you tell us where Azici is?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: It's close to your area of responsibility, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hadzici were in the zone of the 3rd Battalion of the Ilidza Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And in February of 1993 there were efforts to take Azici; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We occupied Azici immediately after Otis, within a very short space of time thereafter. And Otis was taken at the beginning of the war in 1992. I'm not sure of the exact date, but I'm sure that you have it in one of your documents. Give me the date and I'll just tell you whether the date that you have is correct or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. May we have 65 ter 24280, please. This regards the taking of Hadzici and this is a page that's included in the May 1994 report to the Secretary-General regarding the events in Sarajevo. This regards specifically Azici and it includes an interview with you from Reuters dated February 24th, 1993. Would that date remind you of when you took Azici, February 24th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is possible that the document is accurate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was the interview in February or was the occupation of Azici in February? Can we clarify that, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, the representation that I make to the Court is that the interview was in February of 1993. I think the witness has also indicated that the taking was at the same time, but perhaps maybe on re-direct that can be looked into further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So if we look at this part and it's paragraph 1 -- it's the second page of the English, please, but you have it right there in the becoming, it's paragraph 1635. And looking at the English we see it says: "Narrative of events: "Serb forces were reported to have captured the key western suburb of Azici. A Reuters television crew went into the suburb on Tuesday and found it 'completely destroyed.' Heavy fighting broke out nearly two weeks ago when the Serbs attacked the western suburbs. There was speculation that with the fall of Azici fighting would be concentrated in Stup, its BiH-held neighbouring suburb. If the Serbs captured Stup the western entrance to Sarajevo would be wide open. Serb attacks on Azici and Stup followed a BiH government push against the Serb-held stronghold of Ilidza. On some days, more than a thousand shells were reported to have fallen in the contested areas. The Serbs said that they captured Azici without a single soldier killed and only a handful wounded." And this is the quote: "'We don't want to lose more soldiers, so we decided on a new tactic: We destroy a place before we occupy it,' said Svetozar Guzina, deputy commander of the Serb forces in the area." So Mr. Guzina, notwithstanding your ability to target effectively and accurately, here on February 1993 you decided to destroy the whole place, civilian objects and all; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact is that that was not my area of responsibility. The fact is that I was a commander on one axis along which Azici was taken. The fact is that we fired a lot of mortar rounds, and the fact is that in that area there were no civilians. I probably said something to the similar effect. I remember that I provided such a statement. I really don't see a problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6038. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think there have been two occasions where I have shown the witness his 2003 interview in which he was not clear that he actually said what the interview said. The last occasion was the targeting and there was one before that. I would ask to tender just those two particular portions of the 2003 interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you identify the page numbers later on?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I will. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They will be given next Prosecution exhibit number -- it will be. We will just admit them in one batch.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit P6039, so that's a part of 24281.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. West. Do you have any re-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellency. Not many questions, but still I do have some.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Guzina.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear what the President said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I said good morning to everybody including you.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up P01739.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask you to mark the school of theology, the theological institute, could you please make a circle around the building and the usher will provide you with a pen.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that it would be the facility marked with 75. I have a different map in front of me, I believe it's 75.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The usher will help you to circle it and put letters TI next to it.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that that building has three floors. And when it comes to Bosnian Muslim investigators, how did they conclude that fire was opened from there. Was it the number of floors that was decisive in their conclusion?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible because the school of theology is behind our lines and it was the only building with three floors, and the others all had only two floors, the roofs were destroyed, so it was a more dominant building than the others that surrounded it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please refrain from asking leading questions. Your final sentence was so evidently leading. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: In addition to that, Your Honour, he's speaking now about the Bosnian Muslim investigators -- investigation of this incident, which is not something that I spoke about at all. I spoke about the Prosecution's investigation of this incident, so it's beyond the scope.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, Madam West referred to a paragraph in his statement, where it is stated that the Muslim side pin-pointed the school of theology as the source of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, what was the height of the facilities on the front line? How many floors did they have?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we had the old pensioners' home which housed UNPROFOR's bunker for the supervision of the area. We allowed UNPROFOR to set up their bunker there in order to prevent a continuous firing being opened on those lines and for them to finally establish who it was who opened fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you see the old pensioners' home in this map?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The old pensioners' home is somewhere on the front line. I'm not very comfortable with this map; it's different to what I have in front of me. It was some 150 or perhaps 100 metres in front of the theological school, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have --

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, it is the highest building in the whole area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have your firing positions in the old pensioners' home?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, not for a moment throughout the war because the old pensioners' home was inhabited by exclusively elderly people, Muslims, Croats, and Serbs. And I can tell you that on the 6th of June as many as six elderly people died in the course of one day and throughout the war a total of 35 people were killed, and this can be confirmed by UNPROFOR and Milena Mucibabic, who was the lady who was looking after those poor old people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the scale at the bottom of the map which marks kilometres and tell us as an officer how many of these partitions can be placed between the school of theology and the old pensioners' home?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, a lot. A lot of these markings can be fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would it be approximately 2 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1500 metres to 2 kilometres. According to our calculations, it was about 1.5 kilometres between the school of theology and number 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And when we are looking at these houses, is there optical visibility towards number 7?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there's no visibility, optical visibility, because we were not on the roof of the school of theology, we were on the third floor, not on the roof, which means that the visibility was reduced. It was at least 3 metres less than if we had been on the roof, and we could not see a number 7 with a naked eye from the school of theology.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: In line 22 -- 23, it's not registered that I said: A low, ground floor houses on the first line. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, lines 22/23, what page?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 31, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From those low, ground floor houses on the first line, is there optical visibility of number 7?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all. I've just explained that the school of theology was used only for PAT and PAM weapons, which opened fire on Mojmilo Brdo, Alipasino Polje, Dobrinja 2 and 3, and in those grave moments, if I had had any kind of weaponry I would have levelled Dobrinja 5 with the ground if I only could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you ever informed about the trajectory of projectiles in the bus about the levels of the entry hole and the trajectory in the bus itself?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did your soldiers open fire on civilians intentionally on any of -- from any of their positions?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm sure that they didn't. It -- civilians may have been hit by mistake, but I claim with full responsibility that no Serbian soldier intentionally opened fire on civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was there anything that could have distinguished Muslim civilians from a Serb civilian on their side?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we could not make a distinction in any way, especially during the first year and a half. We all wore civilian clothes. Some people wore Territorial Defence uniforms, but more or less all of us were civilians and we walked about in civilians clothes. That's how we came to the front lines. It was only in 1993, the Ilidza Brigade and my battalion finally had uniforms. All of us were finally clad in uniforms, and that was sometime towards the end of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was the height of the buildings on the other side, on the side of the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if the Prosecution says that my positions were the school of theology and the school for the blind, those are three-storey buildings, and across the road I had buildings 10- to 12 floors high. You can imagine yourself that they could have thrown stones at us from those high buildings. You can imagine how we fared at our positions. It was a very specific period of war. If anybody had gone back to see for themselves what the situation was like there, they would be -- they would understand our respective situations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you both slow down and put a pause. Yes, please carry on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED

utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]

utterances.text: But the low building, is that a new or old building? Is this how new buildings are built these days?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that this building is new, that it has been recently built.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Has this photo been tendered into evidence? If it hasn't been, I would like to tender it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now I would like to ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. What would be the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be D2560. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were shown P1601, a document which says that you allegedly admitted that fire was opened and that it wouldn't be opened again. When somebody informed you that your men opened fire, what would be the procedure? Would you immediately deny it or admit it or would you carry out a research, an investigation, in your unit as to what had really happened?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, when UNPROFOR came to my command during the war, I did not have to admit anything before them. They simply came. Perhaps they came on the occasion of what had happened. They told me what had happened. And they said that allegedly the Muslims said that things transpired as purported here. As far as I can remember, they never told me that they ever took part in shedding light on any of those events. It was exclusively what the Muslims told them. They complained against the Serbs. They lodged a complaint against the Serbs, and they were duty-bound to draw our attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can the witness be shown D314.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is. I think that that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 65 ter 11180.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The units of the corps, did they send --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not it. It shouldn't be it. 11280, that would be the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did I directly address brigades or battalions or was it the corps that was the intermediary and that conveyed by orders?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's only natural that the corps would convey your orders to the brigade and then the brigade to the battalion, that is to say to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please identify this. This is the 15th of May, 1993. Can you please take a look at what it says here below, to all units.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ensure that all units and complete personnel of the SRK army are made aware of this and respect this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it clear that they received this as an order from me and then sent it to all units of the SRK?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please focus on paragraph 3. You don't have to read it out loud. Just read it for yourself. Were you aware of this position of the state leadership and of higher commands and was this order being observed?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that that was conveyed to us in the brigade as well and further on towards the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit D2561. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, if you have further questions, I suggest having a break now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you do your military service in the JNA; and if so, did that include education about international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did my military service in the JNA in Bihac, Gospic, in 1979/1980. We did have lectures as far as I can remember. It was a very long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My last question. You mentioned Azici and also you said that there weren't any civilians there. Can you tell us whether there were any soldiers there, or rather, the area was militarised, and what were the facilities that were used as firing positions and positions for fighting against you?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command of the brigade decided only to correct the front line and to link-up our forces with the independent company in Doglodi. The decision was made to reach Azici. In fact, most of this were fields and meadows, but there was this one facility that was called Carapara I think and that was dominant in that area. The Muslim forces were in this area and they were firing at Doglodi and Otis all the time from this Carapara, and the command decided to take that part of the line. We did that efficiently, without any casualties, as stated in this information. I think that we carried out a good operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guzina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Guzina. On behalf of the Chamber, I'd like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. You are free to go and we'll rise all together.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for 30 minutes and resume at ten past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I note that the Prosecution has indicated that it would not respond to the accused's Naser Oric and Ranko Mijic subpoena motions. However, I wonder whether the Prosecution is going to respond to the second motion for subpoena to Eden Garaplija which was filed on 3rd of December, 2012.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't believe so, but if you'll give me a moment to confirm that, that might be the most prudent course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber will now issue an oral ruling on the Prosecution requests in relation to the admission of 65 ter 45111C and 18857A. Turning first to 65 ter 45111C, the Chamber recalls that on the 5th of December, 2012, having noted that in this trial a third party statement may not be admitted unless its content is commented upon, confirmed, or adopted by the witness on the stand, it denied the admission of 65 ter 45111C, a video excerpt depicting Jovan Tintor making a statement through Witness Goran Sikiras. On the same day the Prosecution requested the Chamber to reconsider its decision on the basis that this video should be admitted for the purpose of impeaching Sikiras on the issue of the setting up of barricades. The accused's legal adviser opposed this request on the grounds that, number one, the high standard for reconsideration set by the Chamber had not been met; number two, the video does not actually impeach the witness; and, number three, admitting a videotaped statement which consists of comments made in 1994 by a third person not known to the witness through whom it is presented would be a slippery slope. The Chamber first recalls that it will reconsider one of its decisions in exceptional cases only if the requesting party has demonstrated the existence of a clear error of reasoning or that it is necessary to do so in order to prevent an injustice. Turning now to the substance of the Prosecution's request, the Chamber wishes to clarify that third party statements produced for the purpose of current criminal proceedings may only be admitted pursuant to the modalities of Rules 92 bis, ter, quater, and quinquies. The strict requirements of these rules, which are lex specialis, may not be circumvented by tendering such material pursuant to more general Rule 89. The Chamber refers here to the appeals decision in the Milosevic case issued on the 30th of September, 2002, and the trial decision in the Milutinovic et al. case issued on the 1st of September, 2006. In relation to any other third party statement not prepared for the purposes of criminal proceedings, the Chamber recalls its practice that they may only be admitted if they are commented upon, confirmed, or adopted by the witness on the stand. The Chamber therefore does not consider it has committed an error of law in denying the admission of 65 ter 45111C as the witness could not comment in any way on the video excerpt. In relation to whether the Prosecution has suffered from an injustice that would warrant reconsidering the Chamber's decision, the Chamber notes that the text of Jovan Tintor's statement in the video excerpt was read onto the transcript. Should the Prosecution wish to argue that Tintor's statement impeaches the witness, the Prosecution can refer to the relevant portion of the transcript. The Chamber therefore considers that reconsideration of its decision not to admit 65 ter 45111C is not warranted and denies the Prosecution's request in that regard. Turning now to the admission of 65 ter 18857A, a book excerpt, which was sought by the Prosecution on the 6th of December, 2012, the Chamber notes that the witness on the stand was not able to comment on it in any way. Therefore, for the same reasons as those stated above, the Chamber will not admit 65 ter 18557A into evidence. Unless there are any other matters, we'll bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good afternoon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
