utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you raise it before we have the witness in the courtroom. Yes, please carry on, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. There's a large number of proposed associated exhibits with this witness, some of them -- some of which have not been translated, some of which have not been fully translated, one of which has not been uploaded, a number of which the Prosecution's position is -- are actually irrelevant, and a number of which we feel have been mis-characterised by the witness. And I can go through those to make my position clear now, if I may, and I do that by referring to 65 ter number if that makes it clear enough for everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Going through then the associated documents, as I believe they appear in the statement, the Prosecution's position would be with respect to 1D8362, -63, -64, -65, -68, -70, and -73, that those documents which are a number of combat reports are irrelevant to the case at hand. I just want to note quickly that 1D8374 is now D2512. And with respect to 65 ter number 20843, 1D83 - and please tell me if I should slow down at all - 1D8379, 1 -- pardon me, 65 ter number 18384, 1D8385, 1D8387, 1D8390, -91, those documents, Your Honour, the Prosecution would be requesting that the evidence of the witness related to those documents be led live for a number of reasons, either because the witness has mis-characterised the documents on their face or, indeed, they're not indispensable parts of the witness's statement. In fact, there's no foundation for their admission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- a bit difficult to follow. Let's take a look by way of an example 1D8385, paragraph 98 I take it. "I have been shown document 1D8385 - this is an example that shows that the SRK strictly respected the cease-fire and co-operated with the UNPROFOR ..." and so on. So "this is an example of truthful informing and the document was compiled for the need of the Corps and not for propaganda purposes." So what is your point?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: By way of example with respect to this document, it's not in the witness's document. He doesn't indicate that he's received it or recognises it in any regard, yet he's able to describe it as truthful without any underlying explanation as to why the witness finds it to be truthful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If he finds this paragraph to be truthful, it -- now then it is for you to cross-examine him, isn't it, if he confirms and testifies to the veracity of this paragraph? So what's the point of the Chamber ordering the witness live with respect to this paragraph in more clear terms?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Taking Your Honour's first comment on board and in anticipation of whatever ruling you might make, if you do accept these -- the documents in general, these documents and their explanations, while I'm very conscious of the time-limits directed by this Chamber and make every effort to keep within them, that ruling, allowing for these documents to be accepted and so that I would cross-examine them, might mean that I might be in Your Honour's hands for more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I can understand that you may need more time to deal with this voluminous batch of documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Would I - with respect to the documents that the Prosecution finds irrelevant - be just able to continue down the rest of the list, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 1D6442, 1D6443, 1D6444, 1D6478, and 1D6502, and just to conclude I'd note that 1D6407, 1D6408, 1D6505, 1D6414 are not translated. I stand to be corrected, but 1D8153 has not been uploaded. And I believe the translations of 1D6424 and 1D6447 are incomplete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably I have a different list. Was 1D8153 ever tendered at all?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Reid informs me that that document is not uploaded, but -- so we're unable to check and see whether or not it has been tendered and that may be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The problem is that I don't see that document in the list of associated exhibits. There are many others that you referred to. That also does not appear in the list of associated exhibits, so that's the reason I was confused a bit earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's been a difficult list of associated exhibits to work my way through and any misrepresentations I might have made with respect to the numbers are completely inadvertent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But before we come to the specific issues raised, although you didn't raise it, I want to ask Mr. Robinson what's the problem of all these documents in the sense that they were not listed in your -- in the Defence 65 ter document list at all? Mr. Karadzic couldn't meet the witness in advance or we didn't know that witness would mention these documents, et cetera, cannot be a proper reason to continue such practice until the end of the case. That's just -- that kind of explanation just circumvents the raison d'etre or the reason of the 65 ter rule at all. Do you have any observation, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. First of all, the documents that were not on my Rule 65 ter list were received after this witness was interviewed. This witness was one of the ones that was interviewed rather early, in December of 2011, and so at the time he was interviewed we took the documents that we had identified for him and incorporated them in his statement to the extent that we thought they were important. Afterwards, we received the Rule 66(B) material for him which included these documents. And so it wasn't until before he was interviewed here that we were able to review those documents and find out others -- identify others that we wished to use with this particular witness. And that's why those documents weren't on our 65 ter list and that's why they were added more recently. And we did notify the Prosecution that we were going to be using these documents about a week ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That may be the reason why the Prosecution didn't raise the point of 65 ter list. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's correct, because we've had them for a week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It takes a lot of time. Let's come to the untranslated documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we agree that those -- there are four untranslated documents and we'll lead those live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's identify those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, 1D6407.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: And 1D6505. I'm told that 1D8153 is actually P2419.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that was already admitted. And what were your points, Ms. Edgerton, with respect to the first batch of documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, the first batch of documents that I found to be -- or in my submission are irrelevant, Your Honour, are generally combat reports which either report combat, report a violation of a cease-fire on the part of the ABiH forces, report good relations with UNPROFOR, and -- but for the most part they're characterised by the witness as documents setting out cease-fire violations. And in my view, Your Honours, if -- is that if Dr. Karadzic's case and his defence is that SRK forces under his control only fired back when they were fired at, then these documents showing violations of cease-fires are irrelevant -- or that the witness claims to represent violations of cease-fires are irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, before I hear Ms. Edgerton I was also wondering why the accused should tender a series of similar multiple daily combat reports. In any event, would you like to reply -- respond, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. First of all, these are all reports signed by this witness and they corroborate his testimony, and that's the purpose of associated exhibits is so that you're not left here wondering whether to believe the witness when he says that they were responding to multiple attacks by Muslim forces out -- from the city. And these documents all show the military aims of the Muslim forces and what their activities were, and so it's important for you to understand that this was happening on a daily basis and that they were regularly confronted with attacks from Sarajevo to which they were responding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I take a look at 1D6409 which was referred to in paragraph 140. All the witness said is that this is my document, but I do not know how this is related to that paragraph at all. Similar observation may apply to other paras. Do you have any comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If looking at paragraph 140 when the witness gives a long explanation about the context of this document, that the Muslims wanted to enable tram transport to transport civilians, et cetera, and it shows -- if you look at the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we upload it for the moment. 1D6409. This is it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, so the document indicates that UNPROFOR -- looking at item 3, "UNPROFOR has been engaged in actions in the Nedzarici sector in the home for the blind and in Stup, which is threatening our safety." So this is what he is referring to when he describes how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where in that paragraph does the witness refer to that part?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: He doesn't refer to that part but the paragraph itself refers to their relations with UNPROFOR and why they had -- why they had to essentially do things that were against what UNPROFOR wanted them to do. And the last sentence: "Despite our warnings, the UNPROFOR attempted to set up containers as covers so that we could not observe or engage the military movements of the BiH army." So this essentially relates to item 3 of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the Chamber will proceed in this way. We will order the Defence to lead live with respect to those documents that haven't been translated and other documents will be admitted as part of associated exhibits, but at the same time the Chamber will consider allowing some leeway to the Prosecution in terms of their time for its cross-examination. Let's bring in the witness. But in any event, in para 107 and in para 115 deals with the incident that were not part of the indictment or dropped from the indictment, so I would order the Defence to redact those two paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radojicic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Mr. Radojicic, before you start giving evidence I would like to draw your attention to a particular rule here at the Tribunal. Yeah, under this rule, Rule 90(E), you may object to answering a question from the Prosecution or the accused or from the Judges if you believe that your answer will incriminate you. When I say "incriminate," I mean that something you say may amount to an admission of your guilt for a criminal offence or could provide evidence that you have committed an offence. However, if you think your answer will incriminate you and you do not wish to answer the question, the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. However, in such a case, the Tribunal will make sure that your testimony compelled in such a way shall not be used as evidence in other case against you for any offence other than false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat. We couldn't hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you come closer to the microphone so that the interpreters could hear you. Could you repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I fully understood what you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Radojcic.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.text: Were you retired as a colonel?

utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I will address you as Colonel. Did you give a statement to this Defence team?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I call 1D6900 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you read this statement?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see it before you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.text: I have to remind myself and you to make a short pause between question and answer for the interpreters. Does this statement contain accurately the answers you've given?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC

utterances.text: Have you signed it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.text: If I were to ask the same questions today, would your answers be essentially the same?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to read the summary and then according to the Court's decision I have four documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. We'll give the 92 ter statement the exhibit number first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 1D6900 shall be assigned Exhibit D2562. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And among the associated exhibits there's a map I take it which -- whose 65 ter number is 1D8393. So it's very illegible and we need some translations for the legends. So I would like you to deal with that map live as well in addition to those four untranslated documents. Otherwise, all the other associated exhibits tendered will be admitted into evidence and be given numbers in due course by the Registrar. Please carry on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I should now like to read a brief summary. Colonel Vladimir Radojicic -- before that I'd like to correct a typo. I am pronouncing correctly Radojcic, but the summary is marked Radojicic with an extra i between j and c. It should be deleted. [In English] Vladimir Radojcic worked in Rajlovac as an instructor for defence at the Orao Air Force Institute from April the 6th, 1992, to the 15th of May, 1992. He was transferred to Belgrade where he worked at the Military Academy until the end of 1992. He was commander of the 1st Infantry Ilidza Brigade of the SRK from January 1993 to the end of the war. After the war, he was appointed chief of infantry at the VRS Main Staff where he remained until his retirement on April the 1st, 1998. Colonel Radojcic was aware of the formation of the Green Berets before the war began. The Green Berets were armed with new automatic rifles, pistols, and flak jackets. The 1st Corps of BH army was positioned in the part of the city of Sarajevo under Muslim control in the period between April 1992 and December 1995. The Muslim authorities did not allow the civilians to leave the city and had absolute control over the conditions in the city. His brigade, brigade of Colonel Radojcic, frequently informed the United Nations that the enemy was clearly abusing civilian facilities for military activities. The SRK positions and the civilian population were frequently targeted from the hospital in Dobrinja, for example. No feedback was received and there appeared to be no impact on the forces of the 1st Corps of BH army. The brigade had information that -- and where the units belonging to the 1st Corps of the BH army had command posts, artillery, and positions of -- other fire positions in the depth of their territory. The strategy of the SRK was to protect civilian villages and to prevent a breakthrough of the 1st Corps of BH army which would have had significant impact on other fronts and the course of the war in BH. Vladimir Radojcic's brigade carried out primarily defensive operations. The only offensive operations were carried out to improve tactical positions. His brigade opened fire at the first line of the front and targeted targets in the depth only when they had reliable information that combat elements of the opposed brigade, such as commands, artillery positions, et cetera, were located there. Colonel Vladimir Radojcic received information from superior commands and civilian authorities which was distributed to subordinate units, containing explanations of the provisions of the humanitarian and international law of war. The brigade applied precautionary measures to prevent fire being opened on civilian facilities. Fire was not opened as there was a possibility of civilian casualties, irrespectively of ethnicity. Conversely, the 1st Corps of BH army opened fire at civilians on the territory under the SRK control, especially on the market days, resulting in numerous civilian casualties. This was the case with Muslim sniper fire which was opened on civilians in the city under Serbian control. Neither he nor lower nor superior commands intended to incur civilian victims, terrorise civilians under Muslim control, or exert psychological influence on the civilians. Neither Colonel Vladimir Radojcic nor his brigade were ever ordered by superior commands or civilian authorities, verbally or in writing, to attack civilians or means of the public transport in the city under Muslim control, nor did he issue such orders. Orders from the superior commands were that fire was only to be opened at observed military targets and firing positions. Dr. Karadzic repeatedly pointed out in meetings that any action against civilians or any violation of the international humanitarian law and law of war could have harmful consequences. There was no intention or wish to make civilians' life conditions harder. His brigade's actions were not considered as being part of a systematic or outspread attack on civilians. In Colonel Vladimir Radojcic's brigade there was only one professional serviceman. All the other members of his brigade were local civilians trained mainly for defensive actions which impacted the quality of command and control in the brigade. He also had no professional snipers. The same or similar situation was also in other SRK brigades. Attempts were made to have the paramilitary groups in his zone of responsibility eliminated or disbanded and its members assigned individually to various brigades. The issue of ammunition became increasingly a problem. The orders by the superior commands regarding its use, especially artillery ammunition, were to achieve maximum saving and open fire only when necessary. He had information that modified aerial bombs were used when there was a shortage of ammunition. The bombs were tested and their precision was found to be satisfactory. There were no fuel air explosives in the arsenal of the SRK. Every convoy of humanitarian aid which had been approved by superior commands was allowed to pass and was escorted. In some cases the passage was not approved due to the irregularities, yet even those convoys were also ultimately allowed to pass. He was aware that humanitarian aid was being abused for military purposes of the 1st Corps of BH army or sold in the black market. On one occasion, ammunition was found in the UNPROFOR vehicle destined for the opposing side. President Karadzic decisively forbade any abuse of water, electricity, or gas. Information was received that the Muslim authorities deliberately cut off their supplies when foreign delegations visited. Colonel Radojcic learned that the 1st Corps of BH army used Serbian civilians to dig trenches. Protests were made to international forces. The brigade also had information about the existence of criminal groups within the 1st Corps of BH army. UNPROFOR members were treated correctly and provided with food and correct accommodation and his unit did not consider them hostages but prisoners of war when the conflict between Serbs and UN occur. The conditions were agreed upon through negotiations by all parties. Regarding the incident at the Markale market on 5th of February, 1994, a mixed commission was set up to investigate the incident and Colonel Radojcic was supposed to represent the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. But this commission was not allowed to carry out its work. Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command and the general headquarters and Vladimir Radojcic were certain that the Serbian side was not responsible for it. Regarding shelling incidents in the Klare Cetkin Street and Cetinjska Street on 22nd of January, 1992 [sic], and Safeta Hadzica Street on 26th of June, 1995, and Trg Medjunarodnog Prijateljestva Street on 16th June, 1995, incident of 18 June 1993 - this is out - sniping incident in Djure Jaksica Street on 26th of June, 1994, Colonel Vladimir Radojcic responsibly claims that he never issued orders to open fire at these locations to any units of his brigade nor did he ever receive any feedback information about the alleged attack on these targets. Regarding incident at the junction of Bulevar Avnoja and Nikole Demonje Streets on 25th of May, 1994, Colonel Vladimir Radojcic responsibly claims that he never issued orders to open fire at this location to any units of his brigade, nor did he ever receive any feedback information about the alleged attacks on these target. Moreover, the distance between the two points is beyond the range available in his brigade. Now could I please call into the electronic courtroom 1D06414. [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, could you please focus on 313 and could you tell us how the civilian authorities functioned, when they were established, how they operated, and how that reflected on the operation of the unit and the defence as such.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Even before this decision the civilian authorities had clearly defined work that was clearly aimed at establishing organs of government in the territory of the municipality of Ilidza. As for the relationship with the military, it had to do with logistics for our brigade in the rear. So the relationship between the civilian and military authorities were clearly defined. We did not interfere with each other's work. As for this decision that you asked me about, this relationship became even more operative, that is to say, all the most responsible persons from the area of responsibility of the Ilidza Brigade were in a single place, including the civilian and the military authorities. At these meetings, we made highly operational decisions, and I as brigade commander was only assisted by this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I managed to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- Mr. Karadzic, unfortunately, not knowing the language, the B/C/S, it's very difficult to follow what this document is about. First introduce what this document is about and put your questions later on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: These few decisions here on the establishment of War Presidencies and 313 pertains to Ilidza. Is this a decision on the establishment of the War Presidency of the municipality of Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, it's a leading question although the Prosecution will not challenge it, but it's -- it reduces the probative value of the witness's evidence. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it would also be helpful to know the date of the decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us then please what this document represents. When was it issued and under which circumstances?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: This document was issued on the 20th of June, 1995, at the time of the strongest Muslim offensive that was aimed at deblocking Sarajevo from the external ring.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know all these 14 members?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A moment ago you said that they had all been made available to you for rapid interventions. Do you know what the reason was to establish a War Presidency during this offensive?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: The situation was so critical that decisions had to be made rapidly and carried out as soon as possible. This body made that possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did these people have any other positions or did they hold any other kind of office?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes. I see that the first person referred to here was the president of the municipality and also the president of the War Presidency. And I see representatives of the civilian police and other civilian authorities. As for the army, I was the only one present.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It has no meaning if we don't know who these people are that he's talking about, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I think I -- the first one seems to be Nedeljko Prstojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, sir, could you tell us then, please, what the positions were of these persons, what their positions were among the authorities?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes, very precisely. Number 1, Prstojevic, president of the municipality; number 2 Velibor Veselinovic, his deputy; then Rade Ristic, also a member of the authorities, but on the other side of Ilidza in the area of Vojkovici and Lukavica; then Mr. Djeklic, he had a post in the municipality, I don't remember exactly which one; the late Mr. Lalovic was the financial organ; then Vladimir Radojcic, that's me, from the brigade; 7 Ljubisa Petricevic, commander, commander of the Igman Brigade; Radomir Kojic, at the time commander of the 2nd Sarajevo Brigade; Obren Zeljaja, representative of the authorities of the municipality of Ilidza from the eastern part; Mr. Tihomir Glavas, chief of the Ministry of the Interior; Vlatko Knezevic, also a top person from the Ministry of the Interior; Goran Sehovac, a person who was in charge of communicating with international institutions on behalf of the municipality; Spaso Muratovic, a man who was in charge of mobilisation activities, that is to say, chief of the defence organ; and Slobodan Marilovic, president of the committee of the Serb municipality of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 1D6414 shall be assigned Exhibit D2563, marked for identification pending translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D6408, could we have that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, Colonel, do you know of all the things that we agreed to, what kind of mandate we accepted for the UN forces, for UNPROFOR? Do you know what it was that we had agreed to?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: UNPROFOR had several tasks, both in terms of civilian activity and military activity. As for the military, they supervised the separation lines between my brigade, the 102nd Brigade, the 155th Brigade, and the 104th Brigade of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In addition to this supervision, they toured our positions and they saw for themselves who it was that was violating the agreed cease-fire. We had very specific co-operation with them and the importance I attach to this co-operation is best illustrated by the fact that I appointed a person who had an office at the Serbia hotel and communicated with them on a daily basis. As for their activities in the civilian sector, I am less familiar with them, but I know that they escorted humanitarian convoys that together with other organs of civilian authority they provided humanitarian aid to our population as well as to the population of the Muslim part of Sarajevo, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us whether this is a document of yours and can you tell us what this is about?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, this is barely legible. I can hardly see anything. Maybe if you can remind me, maybe if you can see it better.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll try. The first paragraph says that in the area of Kasindolska gun-fire was opened from the area of Cenex. Do you know what that is?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Cenex is a dominant facility that was on the Muslim positions where there was optical visibility in terms of our positions and especially Kasindolska Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Further down it says, or rather, there's a reference to VRS -- oh, no, oh, no. Already a few times and today as well we warned military observers not to tour -- tour without the presence of our officers. Why was that unacceptable?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: That is correct. We had a liaison officer, an UNPROFOR liaison officer, and we had agreed upon the exact procedure as to how our positions would be toured. Now, this was the procedure: They would report to the officer for co-operation with UNPROFOR; they would express their wish as to the position they wished to tour; then the liaison officer would call the commander, the komandant or komandir of that unit, depending on the number of positions they wished to tour; they would say that they wanted to come; and then they would come. However, in this case obviously this member of UNPROFOR did not observe the required procedure. Why did we react? Because the touring of such positions was very risky for a person that was not familiar with the exact location of land-mines that had been placed along those lines. It is for their safety what we insisted upon the presence of a person of ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, if anything happened to them, what would the consequences be in respect of your own brigade?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Very fortunately this never happened, and I must say that the attitude of UNPROFOR towards the brigade command and vice versa was exceptional. We never had any conflicts that we could not resolve even in the most difficult situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2564, marked for identification pending translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D06407.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please could you tell us if this is also a report of yours and if you could say what it is that this report says. If necessary, I could help you.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask for your help, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's just take a look, it's the 7th of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Aha, can you see it now, can you read it now, the 7th of February, 1994, that's what the stamp says here. Do you see the rest? Enemy: What they did?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: I see that. This is one of our daily reports that we sent to our superior command. This daily report shows that Muslims opened fire at Luzani, and I must say that Luzani is an urban part of Ilidza where only civilians lived. To this day I don't understand why they fired mortar shells, 82-millimetre mortar shells, because there was not a single military target there. Also, I see that they fired at other parts of the front line which was basically something that happened every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the next one that has to do with snipers? Today snipers are operating in all zones; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: I mean, on this day, on this day in question, Muslims opened fire at the entire area of responsibility of the brigade, especially with snipers. When I say "snipers," I am claiming that because the distance between their positions and our positions in the zone of defence of my 2nd Battalion that was outside the urban area in Igman, that's where snipers were used only. So sniper activity was daily practice as far as their forces were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm struggling to understand the relevance of this question. Could you ask the witness to read out the sentence related to snipers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please read this out. The second paragraph, at 2330 in the neighbourhood of Luzani and then further on up to "the sniper."

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: One-third of my copy is illegible. I cannot see it at all. I cannot see the numbers. I cannot read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This sentence that His Excellency, Judge Kwon, asked for that says "today" --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes, "Today at 1300 hours" --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, no, before that. The previous line?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: "During the previous night...," is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, no, just one line above.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: "Snipers are operating along all front lines."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the target of your snipers, those that you had as optical rifles?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: My brigade specifically had 30 snipers. Out of these 30 snipers, half were M76, that is to say real sniper rifles. When I say "real sniper rifles," I mean a sniper rifle with a sniper sight. The remaining 15 were M48 rifles. These were military carbines. And a sight was improvised on these rifles, sights from hunting guns or something like that. So we had a total of 30 snipers. My sniper shooters were mostly deployed in the zone of the 2nd and 3rd Battalion, that is to say outside the built-up areas, for a simple reason, they were more efficient outside built-up areas and using them was more expedient.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say that their snipers were firing at all front lines, does that mean that they had snipers in the areas where you had them?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: They did, for sure. And their activity was particularly pronounced in the neighbourhood of Butmir towards Kasindolska Street, where there was the main intersection of roads, or rather, Kasindolska led between Nedzarici, Ajdonesko [phoen] Naselje and the other parts of Ilidza. So this sniper fire of theirs was the strongest there if you look at the entire war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain why it is that you fired at 10 past 1.00 at Cenex using these shells and you said it was dominant. But what is Cenex? Is it a residential building or something different?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: It is a business building made of concrete where their units were. At this point in time they were involved in a shift of their infantry units and my people noticed that and I ordered that mortar fire be opened against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all unnecessary microphones please be switched off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2565, marked for identification pending translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And I would like to call up 1D06505. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at this document. Does its say here that the enemy on that day mostly respected the cease-fire on lines 2 and 3?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you had an incident on their side at 2350 hours -- there was a provocation; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Those were daily occurrences. There were daily provocations. The front line of my brigade was 22 kilometres long and such cease-fire violations were always possible. We just recorded them and we didn't take any special measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about the line which relates to the convoy?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: It says that the UNPROFOR convoy was let through without any problems. In most of the cases UNPROFOR honoured the procedure for passage and then UNPROFOR convoys passed without any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why did problems arise? When there were problems, what caused them?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: During the war a system was put in place for the passage of UNPROFOR convoys. It had been agreed with my superior command and the liaison officer. Every evening I would thus receive an announcement for UNPROFOR convoys for the following day. In that notification it was specified when the convoy was supposed to pass, the number of vehicles, and the contents of the cargo in the vehicles. And if that was honoured by UNPROFOR and if things were done in that way, there were no problems as far as I can remember. The number of incidents, or rather, the number of problems that we had with UNPROFOR can be counted on the fingers of one hand. Problems arose when things were not honoured, when the agreement was not honoured.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2566 pending translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up the map under 8393.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you assist us with the map, please. And tell us what it depicts.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just for the record this is 65 ter number 1D8393. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D, yes. Can we zoom in on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who issued the map? What does it say?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: The map was issued by the chief of artillery of the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Of which army?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we zoom in on the circle, and that circle depicts Sarajevo itself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, did you make any annotations on the map?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what your annotations represent?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: I drew up the zone of responsibility of my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In what colour?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Red.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This map is obviously linked to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about just admitting 1D8393A, which is a zoomed-up version. I don't think you need this one, given the legibility.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that would be better. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please carry on. I said we would admit the zoomed-up one, then you don't need to cover this if you are not tendering the previous one. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This does not need to be signed. It can be admitted as is; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's part of associated exhibit. Numbers will be given in due course or has been already.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you. And now I would kindly ask for some flexibility. We did not announce the following document, but it ties well with paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- with paragraph 136. I would like to call up 1D6919 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber needs to rise right now. We have a meeting in some context -- some other context. We'll have a break for 45 minutes, Mr. Radojcic. We'll resume at quarter past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.28 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just getting back to the Court concerning the inquiry about the Garaplija request, and we thought we had sent an e-mail indicating that we were not taking a position, but in any event the Court is correct, the same position as the previous motions applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. On the subject of motions for subpoena, it would be helpful if the Trial Chamber could decide the motion concerning Mr. Cutileiro as we are trying to bring him at the beginning of February and making some plans. So if you could turn your attention to that at some point before the recess, we would be greatly appreciative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll consider your submission, Mr. Robinson. Yes, let's continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, in paragraph 136 of your statement you speak about two routes that UNPROFOR could take to get to Sarajevo, one is Sarajevo-Ilidza-Hadzici and the other one is across Mount Igman mountain. What are the differences between these two routes, please?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: The Sarajevo-Ilidza-Blazuj-Hadzici road is an asphalt road which all vehicles use as they go towards Igman and further on towards Bjelasnica. However, Muslims also made a road that went from Igman towards Hrasnica. That road pre-existed, the one that the Muslims made, but it was enlarged and it was ready to accommodate bigger vehicles. We called that road a logistics road because that's how the Muslims got their supplies from the Igman sector to Sarajevo. Obviously 90 per cent of the transports that used that route were military transports. On several occasions, in contact with UNPROFOR, we insisted that UNPROFOR did not use that road, especially not during the night, because we could not control whether the vehicles belonged to UNPROFOR or to the Muslim forces. On several occasions we saw that UNPROFOR vehicles were used as decoy by Muslims who supplied all sorts of things to Sarajevo. That's why we asked UNPROFOR not to use that road during the night and by and large they adhered to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in terms of the distance, which road is better?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: The road leading from Sarajevo via Ilidza, Blazuj, and Hadzici is much shorter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at 1D6119. I apologise. 6919. 1D6919. Thank you. Can we just have one copy and can it be blown up to the maximum. And can some more light be shed on the image, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, do you recognise what is depicted in the photo?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: This photo depicts Mount Igman in the background and closer to me I notice Hrasnica and Sokolovic Kolonija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the usher help the Colonel with the marking and what can you see on Igman?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: I can discern that logistics road coming down from Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I ask the usher to help the witness with the electronic pen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you want me to mark?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, could you please encircle Sokolovic Kolonija and can you put letters SK next to that circle.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now can you mark Hrasnica for us.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You did it in the Cyrillic script. And could you now use the blue pen and mark the contact point between your forces and their forces.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this is the longer line. And what about the line to the right -- [In English] To brush -- to delete this one. No, no, no, the other one. [Interpretation] Can you repeat the one that was erased by mistake and extend it all the way up to the hill, make it a full line?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you are not giving evidence yourself. Ask the witness to do it. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So that was the separation line; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see and did you hear the transports on the Igman road?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: During the night it was particularly well discernible. Lights were dimmed but war lights were on and we could hear the motor vehicles on because they travelled in convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was fire opened on your area of responsibility from Mount Igman, from which parts? Can you see them, can you mark them?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Artillery fire was opened on Ilidza from Igman because one part of the artillery group of the 1st Corps of the BiH army was there and from the Igman sector they opened fire, unfortunately, most commonly on civilian targets. Those were 122-millimetre, 155-millimetre, and 130-millimetre howitzers and guns which were especially destructive --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And could the witness please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Radojcic, you are speaking a bit too fast for the interpreters to keep up. Could you slow down and could -- if you could repeat from -- when you mentioned the 122-millimetre howitzers, could you start from there again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Igman mountain range dominates the Sarajevo valley and there Muslims deployed elements of their corps artillery. I was talking about 122-millimetre howitzers, 155-millimetre howitzers, and 130-millimetre cannon. The last cannon, 130-millimetre cannon, is especially destructive. Its action is very destructive and its non-selective use inflicted huge losses on our forces. On the slopes of Igman Muslim forces were deployed there and they opened machine-gun fire and anti-aircraft fire on the urban parts of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you now please mark the Igman road by putting letters IP next to it and please could you do it in the Latinic script in order not to confuse the participants in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you put the letters IP next to it.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now can I ask you to put a date, today's date, and your signature in the right-hand side corner of this photo.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter document 1D6919 as marked by the witness shall be assigned Exhibit D2618. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellencies. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one thing. Could we upload and see 1D6411 briefly, both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It doesn't look in my pathetic understanding of the language like a translation of the B/C/S document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In my e-court -- that's what I heard, but in my e-court I can see a B/C/S document with the date of 16th of July, 1994, and the format of the document seems to be identical to the English version. But I don't know why it happens. My B/C/S version bears the number Y0006670, but this one is different. So let's leave it there and then we'll come back if necessary. Very well, Mr. Radojcic, as you have noted, most part of your evidence in chief in Mr. Karadzic's case was admitted in a written form in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, Ms. Edgerton. Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You can hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perfect. Thank you. You just left off with Dr. Karadzic talking about a couple of things, and one of them was the Igman road and the other was about weapons held by the ABiH. And I'd like to start off on one of those points and that's about weapons held by your brigade. In addition to the 30 sniper rifles you spoke about with Dr. Karadzic, perhaps you could just confirm the following: Your brigade also had three T-55 tanks?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And those had 100-millimetre guns?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 12.7-millimetre Brownings?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recall how many this far ahead in the future?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 12.7-millimetre, and I have to use the abbreviation, 12.7-millimetre DShK, which I believe stands for Degtyaryov-Shpagin large calibre machine-gun?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was a machine-gun which was part of the standard-issue of the T-55 tanks. It's a 12.7 anti-aircraft machine-gun. But this does not exclude the possibility to use it even more efficiently on ground targets.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You had two 105-millimetre howitzers, at least?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You also had 122-millimetre D30 howitzers?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 122-millimetre howitzers?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 155-millimetre howitzers?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And these guns, these last, those had a range of about 15 kilometres. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the 105-millimetre howitzers had a range of over 10 kilometres; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You had a ZIS 76-millimetre gun?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 120-millimetre mortars?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And your battalions also had 60- and 82-millimetre mortars available to them?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 20- [sic] and 88-millimetre anti-aircraft guns?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: We did not have that calibre anti-armour gun.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Anti-aircraft gun was actually the word I used.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did have that calibre anti-aircraft gun.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: A modified air bomb launcher?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the last stage of the war. When I say "the last stage of the war," I mean 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And 1995 as well?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you had also modified aerial bombs in your arsenal; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And one last question before we go over to the other area we left off, from your statement it's not exactly clear: Did you or did you not have 120-millimetre mortar positions in Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: The battalion fire group in Nedzarici was composed of mortars, 60-millimetre, 82-millimetre, primarily. And due to the complexity and the unfavourable tactical position from the brigade artillery group we attached to them two 120-millimetre mortars in order to be resubordinated to the commander of the 1st Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just to go back to the subject of the Igman road, you spoke to Dr. Karadzic about the differences between the Igman road into Sarajevo and the Sarajevo-Ilidza-Blazuj-Hadzici road, although I think Hadzici comes before Blazuj. And the differences you articulated to Dr. Karadzic, I think, aren't the only differences in those routes. In fact, on the Igman road the difference is that UNPROFOR didn't require your consent or agreement before it entered Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Practical reasons forced us to agree between ourselves on how the road would be used. If the enemy army used that road during the night hours, it was only normal to expect that the commander of the unit took all the necessary measures for that road not to be misused or abused. In order to avoid conflicts with UNPROFOR, we agreed with them that they would be using that road only in daylight. I had to tell you that we had at our disposal information that the 104th Brigade painted its two APCs white and used them also in daylight --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Um --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: -- in the military terminology --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, let me stop you there actually, with respect, Colonel, because you haven't answered my question. And my question was: Is it correct that UNPROFOR using the Igman road didn't require your consent to enter Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And the circumstances that drove UNPROFOR to use that road included the fact that all land routes, all other land routes into Sarajevo had been closed; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we could look at a document. I think P888 would be appropriate. It's a Sector Sarajevo weekly situation report dated 3 June 1995, and there's no translation so we can collapse one side of it. And I'd like to take us to page 3, second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please could we show the witness the date in order to give him the context of the whole situation. Can we go back to page 1, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Noting that I have actually put the date on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But with respect to Colonel Radojcic, could we go back, please, to page 3, second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this document says of the situation in Sarajevo in the second paragraph: "The food situation is steadily deteriorating. The UNHCR contingency stock is nearly exhausted while there have been no land convoys because of the closure of the land routes. The airport remains closed, as the humanitarian air-lift has been suspended for 56 days." Now, do you agree or dispute the assertion in this document or the report in this document about the situation? It notes not only that the land routes have been closed but the air-lift has been suspended for almost two months.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: The very fact that air-lifts of food to Sarajevo were suspended indicates that it was decided at a much higher level than brigade commander. As far as I'm concerned, any movement of the UNPROFOR was not for me to allow or to stop. I could not restrict their use of the road; that was their sovereign right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So actually now seeing this, you don't disagree that all the land routes into Sarajevo had been blocked and the air-lift had been closed?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: I agree that it must have been agreed at a higher level that they should not move and that supplies should be stopped, but it was not within my purview to prevent it or to prohibit it, I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The land routes into Sarajevo, Colonel, were blocked by VRS forces; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: If we look at the map we will see that my neighbour was the Igman Brigade and their neighbour was the Croatian Defence Council. They did not come to our border and I'm telling you I don't know why they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect, that actually doesn't answer my question. It was VRS forces who in April 1995 blocked all land routes into Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see where it's written that it was in April?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think Ms. Edgerton is just simply putting her question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Moving on -- yes, correct. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you answer the question, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot because I don't remember that the road was blocked in the territory of my brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, at this moment can I interrupt you a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me go back to the issue of 1D6411. My apologies. What I saw was 1D6410, so -- and then I noted the translation for 1D6411 is the identical with the translation of 1D6410. So I take it there's no English translation for 6411. So if Mr. Karadzic wants to tender that document, he needs to lead live with the witness about this document. So should I ask Mr. Karadzic to put his question at the end of today's session or shall I ask him to do it now?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It absolutely doesn't matter to me, Your Honour, and it's what Dr. Karadzic would think most appropriate and convenient.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I can do that briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, if you have your statement handy, please look at paragraph 120 and also tell us what does this document say in relation to that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We may collapse the English version because it's not matching with the B/C/S original.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, paragraph 120 does not deal with what Madam Prosecutor asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what does this document deal with?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: If you mean the document from the paragraph 120, it says that Muslims during the cease-fire opened fire at us from several directions along a broad stretch of front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you enumerate these directions?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: From Dobrinja Dvor, Butmir, Stupsko Brdo, and Dobrinja 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What kind of fire was it and what happened and at 2210 hours -- what kind of weapon was used, infantry?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes, infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what about the five shells that hit Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: We're obviously not looking at the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you to read this document.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Oh, the document. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What happened at 2210, or rather, between 2210 and 2230?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: It says five shells landed in the area of Ilidza from the direction of Sokolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you read up to the end, the last sentence?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: There is a black strip on the left. I say -- I only see: "... responded we had no wounded or killed."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 120 you say that it was at a time of a cease-fire. Can you recall that it was at the time of a cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. And as you know, we had many cease-fires and unfortunately very few of them were observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this satisfactory, Your Excellency?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll mark it for identification as D2568 -- no. Shall we give the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It was already assigned Exhibit D2594 marked for identification expending translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I apologise for your confusion, Colonel Radojcic, we had to go back to the Defence examination-in-chief because I found that one document hasn't been translated. Now back to you, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You had indicated you actually didn't know whether all land routes into Sarajevo were closed and I'd like you to have a look at another UN document. It's P822. It's a Sector Sarajevo weekly situation report dated 8 July 1995, and unfortunately again it's not translated but I'll read it to you. The second -- third bullet point on the first page says: "Denied any freedom of movement by the Serbs, UNPROFOR and UNHCR continue to use the Igman road; UNPROFOR and the Bosnians are making joint plans to protect exposed parts of the road with physical barriers. The Serbs seem anxious, and are making some concessions." And if you go over to the top of page 3, please, the first paragraph at the top of page 3 says: "As before, Serb gunners are targeting UN convoys using the Igman road. Every night convoys targeting the road are attacked with machine-guns, cannons, mortars and light field artillery. Very early on Tuesday morning (4 July), two UNPROFOR personnel were injured by shrapnel when bringing humanitarian aid into the city." And if we could go down the page a little bit under the heading: "Igman road used extensively; plans to protect it; Serb concerns," it reads: "Denied any freedom of movement by the Serbs, UNPROFOR and UNHCR have been using the Igman road extensively in the past week. "Two more aid convoys entered the city over Igman during the week, the first on the night of Monday/Tuesday (3/4 July), the second on Wednesday/Thursday (6/7 July). The first was attacked by the Serbs, two drivers were injured and two trucks were damaged. The second convoy came through without incident." Now, this is second document I've shown you which confirms that freedom of movement into the city was denied by the Serbs and as a result UNPROFOR and UNHCR resorted to using the Igman road. Do you still maintain you didn't know that all the land routes into the city had been blocked by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: From what you've read out to me I see that all the incidents that occurred, occurred in the night hours. I must say that we were, after all, at war with the enemy and by night we cannot distinguish whether it's an UNPROFOR vehicle or the Bosnian army vehicle, whether it's a humanitarian aid convoy or the logistical convoy of the BH army. If it were by daylight we could have perhaps made the distinction, but by night we couldn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's fair enough for you to comment upon the Serbs targeting UN convoys, but the question was whether you were aware at -- that all the land routes to Sarajevo were closed or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nobody informed me of that. I repeat, it's possible that it was done at a higher level so that I didn't know. Convoys did not cross the border of Herceg-Bosna. Whether the road was cut off by Herceg-Bosna or the agreement was reached at some different level, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Edgerton, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 87 of your statement, you referred to a document that's D252 and it's a daily combat report from your -- it's an SRK daily combat report on their artillery attack on an unannounced convoy. So just relating that to what you've said, should we understand your evidence -- let me rephrase. Just relating that to the situation you've described, can you tell us what exactly was visible from the 3 kilometres' distance that you fired as reported in this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And we could bring up the document to show the Colonel so he has a chance to see it. It's D2512.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So now your statement says when fire was opened the UNPROFOR vehicle didn't have its light on and the distance from our positions was over 3 kilometres. When we opened fire we didn't know that it was an UNPROFOR vehicle --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a moment, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, Your Honour. Is it only us who are hearing some B/C/S or French? The -- there seems to be a problem. I'm still hearing the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And same over here, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oops, if you could give it a try, Ms. Edgerton -- no, I'm still hearing the -- now I know it's B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm in Your Honour's hands. I'll do whatever I can to accommodate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Possible reason was, Mr. Radojcic, you are too close to the microphone so the sounds from your headphones may be heard by us. Shall we try again. Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Colonel, what exactly was visible from 3 kilometres' distance?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: With the naked eye at 3 kilometres, obviously you couldn't see much. But if you used binoculars, then of course we could see better.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So should we understand your evidence about this use of the Igman road and the targeting of UNPROFOR that its acceptable to fire on a convoy if you can't see it with the naked eye and you don't know it's UN?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: From my report you can see there were two UNPROFOR vehicles and between them there were 12 other motor vehicles. It is therefore evident that it was not just an UNPROFOR convoy, not a purely UNPROFOR convoy, but some combined convoy between UNPROFOR and the Bosnian side. We can see that this is true from the fact that after we opened fire the corps artillery of the 1st Corps opened fire at us from the mountains. Their fire was a response to our fire on the Igman road. I don't think they would have fired if we had only attacked the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, with respect, that's an inference, isn't it, Colonel. So why is it acceptable to fire on a convoy if you don't know that it's the UN?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Because that road was used to transport logistical supplies to the 1st Corps, and the Muslim side very frequently used illicit means. Under international law it's called perfidy. When you abuse the Red Cross and the UNPROFOR, it is a prohibited military ruse that is what happened here.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So in terms of the precautions that you spoke about in your statement several times that you indicated you took to prevent civilian casualties, your evidence then is that in these circumstances those don't apply?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: On what basis am I to know that this is a civilian vehicle and the casualties are civilians?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Doesn't it stand to reason, Colonel, that if you can't see what you're shooting at, you can't determine whether it's the United Nations, you're required to take precautions before opening fire at an object that might risk civilian casualties?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: My communication with the UNPROFOR commander was permanent. I said this at the beginning, we had a liaison officer for the UNPROFOR at the Serbia Hotel in Ilidza. It was always possible to announce that at such and such a time on such and such a day an UNPROFOR convoy would be travelling. This was not done in this case. And you can see that also from the fact that the next day a French colonel from the 2nd Parachute Regiment came to see me and never raised this issue. I remember this very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It was not done - to go back to my point initially - it was not done in this case because land routes were closed. UNPROFOR was effectively a prisoner inside Sarajevo; isn't that correct, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: At that time, if I remember well, UNPROFOR was not our prisoner and all incidents would have been avoided if the liaison officer had been notified. It was in the middle of a war. You don't have many options there. You can allow them or not allow them. If you do allow them, maybe you will pay for it the next day because they would have supplied military equipment; you don't allow it and then you have different problems. Those were situations where you had to make a decision in a second. I always tried, especially in relation to UNPROFOR, to co-operate with them constantly, to deal with all problems through agreement, and most of the time I succeeded. This incident regrettably happened - and I'm saying "regrettably" because it was not inevitable and it wouldn't have happened if we had been notified in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's move on. You talk now again of the liaison officer. Is that Colonel Indjic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Colonel Indjic was the liaison officer for the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. The one with me was Captain Novak Prodanovic, a polyglot who was appointed to that position because of his knowledge of languages and his general culture as an officer. But he was a reserve officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
