utterances.text: Now, protests to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps from the UN for allegations of shelling and sniping against civilians in Sarajevo would go through Colonel Indjic or Colonel Prodanovic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: If they were from the area of activity of my brigade, protests came from both sides. Prodanovic, or rather, the UNPROFOR liaison officer knew both Prodanovic and Indjic. I don't know which incident you are now referring to, but we never sniped at civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So Indjic not only had something to do with receiving protests from UNPROFOR, he had something to do - it seems from your answers to Dr. Karadzic - with freedom of movement as well because you described a procedure that UNPROFOR had to follow for visiting your positions?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we'll move on to another area and that's about the modified air bombs that you spoke about at the beginning of your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you would agree with me that air bombs per se are aerial weapons that are designed to engage area targets, not small targets at all; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: I was lucky enough in my military career to spend some time in the air force, so I know a bit more than an average infantry officer. The air force had several types of weaponry including air bombs. There was several types of air bombs depending on the target. This one was a type of air bomb that was designed for destroying personnel and equipment in closed spaces and buildings, contact fuse air bombs.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you're referring to the different kinds of air bombs now in possession of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, is it your evidence that 100 -- the 100- and 250-kilo air bombs were designed for destroying personnel and equipment in closed spaces and buildings?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Contact fuse bombs, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What kind of destructive -- actually, the destructive power of these bombs, 100- and 250-kilos is massive; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: When we say contact fuse aerial bombs weighing 100 kilos, we have to know that the explosive charge accounts for 40 per cent of the total weight of the bomb. The rest is the body of the aerial bomb and that after the explosion during which the bomb is fragmented, of course this is massive. Yes, it's a powerful bomb.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: As a professional military officer, you were - and since you know something about air bombs - you must know that weapons testing in the arms industry in the former Yugoslavia was very demanding and required the firing of a significant number of missiles to produce firing tables?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact, sometimes hundreds of firings before the firing tables are produced and the weapons finally approved.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So when you said in your statement that both the missile engines and the whole kit were tested, you mean they were tested by firing?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it was not fired on personnel. It was done at the Kalinovik testing ground which is an old artillery testing ground. Only after those testings were we allowed to use such bombs.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How many times was it fired?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: If you mean in the area of responsibility of my brigade --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No. In testing. How many times was it fired?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I can't tell you that. However, if we received the so-called temporary firing tables, that means that those who delivered the firing tables to us had some relevant information based on which he was of the opinion that launching the bombs from launchers was okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you have no information as to any testing that was done to the same exigencies as would have been the case in the normal arms industry of the former Yugoslavia? You don't know? Or to the same exigencies, pardon me.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I can't answer your question because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you said the deviation range was 10 metres by 1.000. Do you actually have a firing table that supports that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: No, I don't have that firing table. It was the chief of artillery who had it. Based on those firing tables, they calculated targeting elements. You could not just place a rocket on the -- on a launcher, turn it towards the target, and do things approximately. It had to be done by means of firing tables and -- but those firing tables were only temporary.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Two questions. Just to go back to something you said earlier, you talked about testing at the Kalinovik testing ground. Do you know that because you attended the testing of the air bombs there?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: I wasn't there. I was a brigade commander and that was within the purview of the centre who dealt with that. I was not there but I know based on the fact that we received those tables that testing and test firings should have been done and that a number of bombs had to be fired first before the tables could be compiled. I myself was not there at the testing ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So who's the chief of artillery who had them, the firing tables?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: The chief of artillery of the Ilidza Brigade was Predrag Bosicic, that was his name. And the artillery battalion commander was Bosko Radijgljac.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So he had the firing tables but you haven't got them?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: I was the brigade commander. In order to make my work easier, according to our establishment, the brigade commander had at his disposal chief of artillery, communications, and other branches. They were those professionals that assisted a commander in arriving at the right decision. In other words, this was a professional issue that was within the purview of the chief of artillery, and I as the brigade commander did not have to deal with that at all and I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you didn't deal with that but you know something about these modified air bombs. You know, for example, that they were powered by rockets?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I can remember. We used rockets that were used by the Plamen multi-rocket launcher. They were used as the fuelling agent.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact, would you agree that there were different numbers and different types of rockets actually used with the air bombs?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: I can't answer your question precisely because this is beyond the scope of my knowledge and my authority on aerial bombs.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So -- but when you talk about the deviation of the bombs and say that it's similar to mortars, well, I'd like to explore that, actually. I want to talk about the emission of the rockets, for example. So if a rocket -- if a bomb is using more than one rocket and a rocket ignites -- one of those rockets ignites even tenths of a second after the other rockets, you would agree that that would cause a deviation in the course of the modified air bomb, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether a deviation is possible in the timing of igniting of various bombs, but I don't think it is possible. Those bombs were precise, deviations were minimal. But as any projectile which has an in-flying trajectory, we're talking about possible deviations. We can talk about them primarily due to meteorological conditions such as wind, humidity, and so on and so forth, but all those are conditions which have already been taken into account and can be found as being incorporated in firing tables.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you just said you don't know anything about whether a deviation is possible in the timing of igniting, but you don't think so, but you said deviations were minimal. So let me put this to you: What if actually two rockets ignite at two different times, that's going to create another and maybe even a greater deviation, won't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: I said that I thought it was technically impossible for those rockets to be ignited one by one because there's needle that would ignite all four rockets or two -- it depended on how many a launcher can take. Please bear in mind that I'm an infantry officer. This is not my area of expertise.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if a rocket is launched or in the launching a rocket deviates somewhat, you would agree that the longer the flight the potential for greater deviation, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland [sic], this -- I mean, this is all really self-evident stuff, isn't it? I mean if something goes wrong with a rocket and it doesn't fly a true course, it will deviate. The question really is: Did that happen? Sorry, I called you Ms. Sutherland. That wasn't rocket science.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's not a problem, Your Honour. And taking your words into account, could I just have a couple of moments to look back at the transcript and one of the colonel's answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You've said deviations were minimal. Does that mean -- do you say that on the basis of the reports you received on the rocket explosions?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: For those rockets that were launched and of which I was aware, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm going to return to this but I need to -- I'm going to return to this in a different way and I just need to consult my notes for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Talking about some of the incidents you discussed in your statement, you talked about an incident you wrote, actually, about an incident on 26th June 1995 that occurred in Safeta Hadzica Street and said that it occurred in the midst of a fierce offensive and that you never received any feedback about the attack. Now, I suggest to you that you never received feedback because the incident actually took place on 26 May 1995.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Fine. We can move on further. At a couple of points in your statement you highlighted that your brigade members local civilians who needed training, they were -- your officers and command staff were untrained for performing their duties and that had a significant impact, you said, on command and control. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In that regard let's have a look at an order that you -- an order of General Milosevic's that you commented on in your statement. It's P1201 and it's dated 6 April 1995. This is an order to your brigade to thwart the enemy and give them a warning so they're forced to accept a truce and ordering your brigade to prepare a launcher with an aerial bomb and select the highest-yielding target in Hrasnica or Sokolovic Kolonija where there will be the greatest human and material losses. So my question to you is: Even though you insisted in your statement that the order that civilians should not be attacked was so important that it was constantly repeated, it's not repeated here. Doesn't this reflect an assumption that the people who implemented the order knew exactly what they were going to do?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: In military terminology, when you want to open fire on enemy personnel, you use that term, live personnel. When a general orders me to open fire on personnel, on soldiers, the way I understand that order is to open fire on the enemy soldiers, exclusively on the enemy --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: -- soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- Colonel, that's an order for bodies. It doesn't say anything about military targets.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: The system of command was such that in an ops room there was a map belonging to the chief of artillery. It was a working map. And on that map there were markings for all those targets that our artillery was supposed to fire upon. There were numbers and different other markings. So when General Milosevic told me: Open fire on a target which will inflict the biggest number of casualties among the personnel, the way I understood it was to open fire on the place where at that moment there was the highest number of personnel. In this specific case it was their command.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So that order -- your evidence is that that order leaves you free to point the air bomb wherever you want to ?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Yes -- well, yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, given that, given --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be allowed to finish his answer? I was not allowed to interrupt him mid-sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Fair enough. Let's hear him out. Do you have anything further to add, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I expected that there will be an even more precise question when I was interrupted, which is why I actually stopped myself continuing my answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Colonel, given that you've already said that your brigade is local civilians, untrained, your officers were untrained, the lack of training had a significant impact on the quality of command in your brigade, we can't have any confidence that the people who implemented this order knew exactly what to do?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: When I described how my brigade was set up and who its members were, this is precisely what I said. My men were locals and there were very few professional career officers in that brigade. I was the only one in addition to the chief of the anti-aircraft artillery. I was the only active-duty officer, which doesn't mean that my chief of artillery and battalion commander who completed reserve military schools for artillery were not trained to carry out the duties that were assigned to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What I'd like to put to you is that General Milosevic could have no confidence, especially given that the order to pay special attention to civilians was not repeated here, he could have no confidence that the order -- this order - which you've already characterised as incomprehensible to anyone but a professional officer - no confidence that a target could be properly engaged, giving due consideration to the civilians who might be in the area?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: I must tell you that according to the international law of war, unit commanders during combat in a built-up area are duty-bound to move out civilians from combat areas. In the first part of this order it says that for three days Muslim forces had been attacking the 2nd Sarajevo Brigade, which means that a commander of the Muslims 4th Brigade, Fikret Prevljak, had been attacking a Serbian brigade for three days. He was duty-bound to move out civilians according to the international law of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Failure to act according to IHL, Colonel, doesn't excuse the other party for failing to do the same; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: The number of casualties, does it not speak volumes that I did to the best of my abilities, just like you think that I should have, after the launching of that aerial bomb.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to offer a better interpretation. Instead of he was "forced," I would use the word "he was obliged to move the civilians out of the combat area."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, just one more document for today, Your Honours, and that's 1D8436, which is dated 5 August 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Which you also referred to in your statement in reference to the document we've just been discussing. And it's a document by your fellow brigade commander suggesting economic and military targets to the SRK command in retaliation for an incursion into SRK territory. And your fellow brigade commander is Mr. Sehovac. Now, is this your target list, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: As far as I can tell, the target of my brigade was only the command post of the 4th and later on the 104th Motorised Muslim Brigade. The command post which was in the Hrasnica school.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is your evidence that your target is then based on a document that's dated a full eight months before the incident we're discussing?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Throughout the war the post office in Hrasnica was the communications centre and the main command post for the 4th and later on 104th Brigade of the BiH army brigade. Next to it, the Aleksa Santic school which is mentioned in here was the facility where special units of the 1st Corps were trained. It was also the place where ammunition was being manufactured for a little while during the war. We managed to learn that -- I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we see next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So this document which referred to in reference to General Milosevic's document P1201 actually has no reference to P1201 eight months later at all, does it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: I did not understand your question. I don't know what document you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We were discussing --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Could you please --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sure. We were discussing the document issued by -- the order issued by Dragomir Milosevic on 6 April 1995 to launch an air bomb at the most profitable target in Hrasnica or Sokolovic Kolonija. And this document which you referred to in your evidence actually has no relation to any target selection you might have done eight months later, does it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: All our targets in Hrasnica were more or less permanent targets. Throughout the war they were always there. So nothing had changed in those eight months. In order to exclude the possibility of making an error, I could always resort to intelligence work and learn from those who defected about any even minor changes to the targets that were marked on the map of the chief of artillery. All that simply excluded any possibility of a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But there was a mistake that happened on the 6th of April, 1995, because you didn't hit the targets, did you? You hit a private house.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: Which target?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You didn't hit the post office building in Hrasnica, you didn't hit the Aleksa Santic primary school in Hrasnica; on the 6th of April, 1995, you hit a private house?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC
utterances.text: I apologise about that imprecision of 20 metres. That house was 20 to 30 metres away from the facility which was our target. It was not a civilian house. It may have been during -- before the war, but during the war this was where their guards were billeted, those who provided security for the command. According to information that I received from UNPROFOR, only one soldier was hit. He told me that he had seen with his own eyes that the man wore a uniform, so after all you will have to admit that we were precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, I see the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, and it would be a very good time to break. I estimate that tomorrow I would probably be half an hour further and no longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Radojcic, we will adjourn for today. I'd like to advise you about the rule here at the Tribunal, that you are not supposed to discuss about your testimony with anybody else. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll resume tomorrow at 9.00. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 12th day of December, 2012, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.48 p.m.,
